Industry observers note that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

Sources indicate that this tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

In a recent development, the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

It has been revealed that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint indicates so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

It has been revealed that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

In a recent development, here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Sources indicate that every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

It has been revealed that setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

It has been revealed that now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Industry observers note that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Sources indicate that don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to customers later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

According to recent reports, store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF indicates what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

In a recent development, A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

Industry observers note that in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

Sources indicate that in the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Two months since releasing our first batch of Holo2 models, H Organization is back with our largest UI localization model yet: Holo2-235B-A22B Preview. This model achieves a new State-of-the-Art (SOTA) record of 78.5% on Screenspot-Pro and 79.0% on OSWorld G.

Available on Hugging Face, Holo2-235B-A22B Preview is a research release focused on UI element localization.

It has been revealed that high-resolution 4K interfaces are challenging for localization models. Small UI elements can be difficult to pinpoint on a large display. With agentic localization, however, Holo2 can iteratively refine its predictions, improving accuracy with each step and unlocking 10-20% relative gains across all Holo2 model sizes.

Holo2-235B-A22B's Performance on ScreenSpot-Pro.

Holo2-235B-A22B Preview reaches 70.6% accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro in a single step. In agent mode, it achieves 78.5% within 3 steps, setting a upcoming state-of-the-art on the most challenging GUI grounding benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that training Holo2 models at scale requires coordinating workloads across multiple cloud providers. H Firm uses SkyPilot as a unified interface for launching training jobs on our clusters with Kubernetes (k8s). By abstracting away infrastructure complexity, SkyPilot lets researchers focus on model development instead of managing k8s manifests or maintaining separate deployment scripts.

  • It has been revealed that let's be real about where we are with evals in 2026.
  • Furthermore, there is another gap within reported benchmark scores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: Benchmark datasets on Hugging Face can now host leaderboards. Models store their own eval scores. Everything links together. The community can submit results via PR. Verified badges prove that the results can be reproduced.

It has been revealed that let's be real about where we are with evals in 2026. MMLU is saturated above 91%. GSM8K hit 94%+. HumanEval is conquered. Yet some models that ace benchmarks still can't reliably browse the web, write production code, or handle multi-step tasks without hallucinating, based on usage reports. There is a clear gap between benchmark scores and real-world performance.

Furthermore, there is another gap within reported benchmark scores. Multiple sources report different results. From Model Cards, to papers, to evaluation platforms, there is no alignment in reported scores. The result is that the community lacks a single source of truth.

Decentralized and transparent evaluation reporting.

Industry observers note that we are going to take evaluations on the Hugging Face Hub in a new direction by decentralizing reporting and allowing the entire community to openly report scores for benchmarks. At first, we will start with a shortlist of 4 benchmarks and over time we’ll expand to the most relevant benchmarks.

For Benchmarks: Dataset repos can now register as benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE are already live). They automatically aggregate reported results from across the Hub and display leaderboards in the dataset card. The benchmark defines the eval spec via eval.yaml, based on the Inspect AI format, so anyone can reproduce it. The reported results need to align with the task definition.

Sources indicate that for Models: Eval scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml in the model repo. They appear on the model card and are fed into benchmark datasets. Both the model author’s results and open pull requests for results will be aggregated. Model authors will be able to close score PR and hide results.

For the Community: Any user can submit evaluation results for any model via a PR. Results get shown as "community", without waiting for model authors to merge or close. The community can link to sources like a paper, Model Card, third-party evaluation platform, or inspect eval logs. The community can discuss scores like any PR. Since the Hub is Git based, there is a history of when evals were added, when changes were made, etc. The sources look like below.

To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

In a recent development, decentralizing evaluation will expose scores that already exist across the community in sources like model cards and papers. By exposing these scores, the community can build on top of them to aggregate, track, and understand scores across the field. Also, all scores will be exposed via Hub APIs, making it easy to aggregate and build curated leaderboards, dashboards, etc.

Community evals do not replace benchmarks so leaderboards and closed evals with published results are still crucial. However, we believe it's crucial to contribute to the field with open eval results based on reproducible eval specs.

According to recent reports, this won't solve benchmark saturation or close the benchmark-reality gap. Nor will it stop training on test sets. But it makes the game visible by exposing what is evaluated, how, when, and by whom.

According to recent reports, mostly, we hope to make the Hub an active place to build and share reproducible benchmarks. Particularly focusing on latest tasks and domains that challenge SOTA models more.

Read the docs: To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

Add eval results: Publish the evals you conducted as YAML files in .eval_results/ on any model repo.

Check out the scores on the benchmark dataset.

Register a fresh benchmark: Add eval.yaml to your dataset repo and contact us to be included in the shortlist.

Recent findings suggest that the feature is in beta. We're building in the open. Feedback welcome.

Great initiative, aggregating multiple signals is the way to go!

Although such a measure has not solved the problems encountered in the current evaluation, at least it is indeed a very good measure in terms of decentralization and mobilizing the power of the community for co-construction.

Will there be the integration with existing huggingface lighteval?

Industry observers note that hi @naufalso ! Lighteval now suport inspect-ai as a backend, so everything supported by inspect is integrrated in lighteval 🔥.

This is a very crucial and timely initiative. It’s easy to get lost in the sea of leaderboards, each with its own format and reporting style. The Inspect AI log format brings much‑needed standardization, and having Hugging Face host evaluation logs is a real game changer. One reason many valuable benchmarks fade away is that original contributors often lack the resources to continuously maintain leaderboards. The Community Evals initiative has tremendous potential to address this gap, and I truly appreciate the effort behind it.

We’re hoping to include our planning benchmark, ACPBench, as part of this ecosystem—it's fully compatible with Inspect AI, the evaluation scripts are available on our GitHub.

SyGra 2.0.0 introduces Studio, an interactive environment that turns synthetic data generation into a transparent, visual craft. Instead of juggling YAML files and terminals, you compose flows directly on the canvas, preview datasets before committing, tune prompts with inline variable hints, and watch executions stream live—all from a single pane. Under the hood it’s the same platform, so everything you do visually generates the corresponding SyGra compatible graph config and task executor scripts.

Let’s walk through this experience step by step.

Industry observers note that open Studio, click Create Flow, and Start/End nodes appear automatically. Before adding anything else:.

Once validated, Studio keeps the configuration in sync and pipes those variables throughout the flow—no manual wiring or guesswork.

In a recent development, drag the blocks you need from the palette. For a story-generation pipeline:.

Sources indicate that studio’s detail panel keeps everything in context—model parameters, prompt editor, tool configuration, pre/post-process code, and even multi-LLM settings if you want parallel generations. Typing { inside a prompt surfaces every available state variable instantly.

Open the Code Panel to inspect the exact YAML/JSON Studio is generating. This is the same artifact written to tasks/examples/, so what you see is what gets committed.

After the run, download outputs, compare against prior executions, get metadata of latency and usage details.

SyGra Studio can also execute existing workflow in the tasks. For example, in the tasks/examples/glaive_code_assistant/ workflow — it ingests the glaiveai/glaive-code-assistant-v2 dataset, drafts answers, critiques them, and loops until the critique returns “NO MORE FEEDBACK.”.

SyGra Studio turns synthetic data workflows into a visual, user friendly experience. Configure once, build with confidence, run with full observability, generate the data without ever leaving the canvas.

Sources indicate that syGra Studio looks like a powerful platform for synthetic data generation workflows! For teams working with complex data pipelines like this, clear system documentation is essential. I've been using InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) to document our ML infrastructure—you describe your system architecture in plain English and it generates diagrams that you can refine conversationally. It's been really helpful for onboarding upcoming team members and creating design docs that actually stay current with our evolving architecture.

SyGra Studio is a legit unlock: visual graph workflows that remove the pain of hand-editing YAML. Good work!

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

Recent findings suggest that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Sources indicate that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

Recent findings suggest that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly key when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Sources indicate that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two crucial parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/owners.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Sources indicate that runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

It has been revealed that swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a upcoming optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

Sources indicate that however, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

Industry observers note that this becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Industry observers note that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

According to recent reports, you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

Tech Report: Transformers.js v4: Now Available on NPM!

📅 09 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM!
  • The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a new WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++.
  • Industry observers note that in addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this latest WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM! After a year of development (we started in March 2025 🤯), we're finally ready for you to use it.

The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a new WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++. We've worked closely with the ONNX Runtime team to thoroughly test this runtime across our ~200 supported model architectures, as well as many new v4-exclusive architectures.

Industry observers note that in addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this latest WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications. That's right, you can now run WebGPU-accelerated models directly in Node, Bun, and Deno!

We've proven that it's possible to run state-of-the-art AI models 100% locally in the browser, and now we're focused on performance: making these models run as fast as possible, even in resource-constrained environments. This required completely rethinking our export strategy, especially for large language models. We achieve this by re-implementing new models operation by operation, leveraging specialized ONNX Runtime Contrib Operators like com.microsoft.GroupQueryAttention, com.microsoft.MatMulNBits, or com.microsoft.QMoE to maximize performance.

For example, adopting the com.microsoft.MultiHeadAttention operator, we were able to achieve a ~4x speedup for BERT-based embedding models.

Developing a fresh major version gave us the opportunity to invest in the codebase and tackle long-overdue refactoring efforts.

Recent findings suggest that until now, the GitHub repository served as our npm package. This worked well as long as the repository only exposed a single library. However, looking to the future, we saw the need for various sub-packages that depend heavily on the Transformers.js core while addressing different use cases, like library-specific implementations, or smaller utilities that most owners don't need but are essential for some.

That's why we converted the repository to a monorepo using pnpm workspaces. This allows us to ship smaller packages that depend on @huggingface/transformers without the overhead of maintaining separate repositories.

In a recent development, another major refactoring effort targeted the ever-growing models.js file. In v3, all available models were defined in a single file spanning over 8,000 lines, becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For v4, we split this into smaller, focused modules with a clear distinction between utility functions, core logic, and model-specific implementations. This fresh structure improves readability and makes it much easier to add new models. Developers can now focus on model-specific logic without navigating through thousands of lines of unrelated code.

In v3, many Transformers.js example projects lived directly in the main repository. For v4, we've moved them to a dedicated repository, allowing us to maintain a cleaner codebase focused on the core library. This also makes it easier for users to find and contribute to examples without sifting through the main repository.

We updated the Prettier configuration and reformatted all files in the repository. This ensures consistent formatting throughout the codebase, with all future PRs automatically following the same style. No more debates about formatting... Prettier handles it all, keeping the code clean and readable for everyone.

Thanks to our latest export strategy and ONNX Runtime's expanding support for custom operators, we've been able to add many new models and architectures to Transformers.js v4. These include popular models like GPT-OSS, Chatterbox, GraniteMoeHybrid, LFM2-MoE, HunYuanDenseV1, Apertus, Olmo3, FalconH1, and Youtu-LLM. Many of these required us to implement support for advanced architectural patterns, including Mamba (state-space models), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Perhaps most importantly, these models are all compatible with WebGPU, allowing customers to run them directly in the browser or server-side JavaScript environments with hardware acceleration. We've released several Transformers.js v4 demos so far... and we'll continue to release more!

We've migrated our build system from Webpack to esbuild, and the results have been incredible. Build times dropped from 2 seconds to just 200 milliseconds, a 10x improvement that makes development iteration significantly faster. Speed isn't the only benefit, though: bundle sizes also decreased by an average of 10% across all builds. The most notable improvement is in transformers.web.js, our default export, which is now 53% smaller, meaning faster downloads and quicker startup times for users.

Version 4 also adds upcoming library features that make it easier to build robust, production-ready applications.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh ModelRegistry API is designed for production workflows. It provides explicit visibility into pipeline assets before loading anything: list required files with get_pipeline_files, inspect per-file metadata with get_file_metadata (quite useful to calculate total download size), check cache status with is_pipeline_cached, and clear cached artifacts with clear_pipeline_cache. You can also query available precision types for a model with get_available_dtypes. Based on this new API, progress_callback now includes a progress_total event, making it easy to render end-to-end loading progress without manually aggregating per-file updates.

Sources indicate that we also added upcoming environment controls for model loading. env.useWasmCache enables caching of WASM runtime files (when cache storage is available), allowing applications to work fully offline after the initial load.

env.fetch lets you provide a custom fetch implementation for use cases such as authenticated model access, custom headers, and abortable requests.

In a recent development, finally, logging is easier to manage in real-world deployments. ONNX Runtime WebGPU warnings are now hidden by default, and you can set explicit verbosity levels for both Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. This update, also driven by community feedback, keeps console output focused on actionable signals rather than low-value noise.

Sources indicate that A frequent request from owners was to extract the tokenization logic into a separate library, and with v4, that's exactly what we've done. @huggingface/tokenizers is a complete refactor of the tokenization logic, designed to work seamlessly across browsers and server-side runtimes. At just 8.8kB (gzipped) with zero dependencies, it's incredibly lightweight while remaining fully type-safe.

This separation keeps the core of Transformers.js focused and lean while offering a versatile, standalone tool that any WebML project can use independently.

Sources indicate that we've made several quality-of-life improvements across the library. The type system has been enhanced with dynamic pipeline types that adapt based on inputs, providing better developer experience and type safety.

In a recent development, additionally, we've added support for larger models exceeding 8B parameters. In our tests, we've been able to run GPT-OSS 20B (q4f16) at ~60 tokens per second on an M4 Pro Max.

We want to extend our heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to this major release, especially the ONNX Runtime team for their incredible work on the latest WebGPU runtime and their support throughout development, as well as all external contributors and early testers.

OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.
  • OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments.
  • In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

OpenEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that openEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?".

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

In a recent development, to ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across owners and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Recent findings suggest that below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

It has been revealed that multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Sources indicate that ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

It has been revealed that correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

Recent findings suggest that for a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

In practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring challenges.

It has been revealed that below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

The agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

Industry observers note that we can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real people can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

According to recent reports, the Free strategy is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app people, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every blueprint, Free included.

Sources indicate that the questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Sources indicate that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real firm data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. According to recent reports, agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human customers.

Recent findings suggest that building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

According to recent reports, the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

It has been revealed that writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

According to recent reports, we gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

It has been revealed that the Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:.

We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end. We benchmarked the kernels and found that the optimized kernels can provide a speedup in both isolated and end-to-end performance.

According to recent reports, AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Recent findings suggest that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

In a recent development, • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

Industry observers note that • Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page demonstrates different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and notes other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and blueprint prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

It has been revealed that copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Recent findings suggest that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, indicates very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Recent findings suggest that turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

It has been revealed that strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Industry observers note that limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. In a recent development, sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page states false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Sources indicate that the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

According to recent reports, • Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. Upcoming models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

Industry observers note that openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

Recent findings suggest that • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

It has been revealed that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and upgrade as fresh models appear.

Industry observers note that • Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

In a recent development, • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

According to recent reports, • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Industry observers note that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

In a recent development, sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

Industry observers note that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

Recent findings suggest that AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

Industry observers note that pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

Recent findings suggest that spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ayhan Sebin Saurabh Jha Rohan Arora Daby Sow Mert Cemri Melissa Pan Ion Stoica.

ITBench HF Space ITBench HF Dataset MAST HF Dataset ITBench Github MAST Github.

IBM Research and UC Berkeley collaborated to study how agentic LLM systems break in real-world IT automation, for tasks involving incident triage, logs/metrics queries, and Kubernetes actions in long-horizon tool loops.

Benchmarks typically reduce performance to a single number, telling you whether an agent failed but never why. To solve this black-box problem, we applied MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), an emerging practice for diagnosing agentic reliability ). By leveraging MAST to analyze ITBench—the industry benchmark for SRE, Security, and FinOps automation—we turned raw execution traces into structured failure signatures, revealing exactly what broke and how to fix it. We annotated 310 ITBench SRE traces across three distinct model classes: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Takeaways from our analysis when building agents:.

If you’re building agents for enterprise IT workflows, this is the kind of evaluation you want: not just “did it pass?”, but “what broke, where, and what intervention is most leverageable?”.

Industry observers note that benchmarks like ITBench are becoming the standard for measuring agentic performance in high-stakes IT automation tasks. In ITBench, agents act as Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) or Security Analysts tasked with diagnosing Kubernetes outages, patching vulnerabilities, or managing cloud costs in production environments.

Recent findings suggest that this benchmarks use success rate as a main metric to evaluate agents. However, this metric is insufficient for engineering robust systems. Knowing that an agentic system achieves a 14% success rate on ITBench tells us that it failed, but not why: Did it fail because it forgot the context? Because it hallucinated a command? Or because it simply did not terminate?

Without a comprehensive approach to diagnose these failures, developers are left guessing, often resorting to blind prompting tweaks that solve one problem only to create another.

As a fresh standard to analyze the failure modes of complex agentic systems, we developed MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy). MAST brings more insights and open up the opaque evaluation of these benchmarks. Derived from a rigorous analysis of over 1,600 traces across seven different frameworks, MAST provides a standardized taxonomy for agent failures.

MAST converts unstructured execution logs into structured "failure vectors" based on 14 distinct patterns across three key categories:.

We stress-test the idea of using MAST to make agent evaluations actionable and gain insights on the failure modes by applying it to ITBench, a popular evaluation suite for IT automation tasks across SRE, Security/Compliance, and FinOps.

We annotated 310 ITBench SRE execution traces produced by an SRE agent built with Codex in realistic environments. These traces capture natural language interactions between agents and their tools across three models representing different capability tiers: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B. This lets us look past simple success metrics and investigate the distinct failure signatures driving these results. For this we use the recall scores, as the models by design only output a maximum of 3-5 outputs and SREs prefer the recall scores over F-1 score.

Below, we detail the findings from this diagnostic analysis.

When we examine the failed traces, a clear hierarchy of complexity becomes apparent across the three models. This is measured by the number of distinct failure modes observed per failed run.

This disparity in failure mode density reveals a fundamental difference in how these systems break down. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a surgical failure profile. Even in unsuccessful runs, it maintains high internal coherence and typically fails due to a single isolated failure, such as an incorrect verification step. These failures are precise and far easier to diagnose.

Sources indicate that on the opposite end of the spectrum, GPT-OSS-120B suffers from cascading collapse. In these traces, we observe that errors tend to compound over time. A small reasoning mismatch early in the process often leads to a deviation from the task specification, which in turn triggers a total derailment of the agent. Kimi-K2 represents the middle ground, where failures are more frequent and complex than the frontier model but do not reach the systemic instability seen in the 120B open weights model.

The significance of this finding is that a higher success rate is often accompanied by isolated failure. Systems that fail with fewer simultaneous problems are far more predictable and simpler to improve through targeted engineering interventions.

According to recent reports, perhaps the most critical insight from MAST is distinguishing between failures that the system can tolerate versus those that are fatal to success of the downstream task. By comparing the distribution of failure modes in Successful Traces vs. Failed Traces, we can classify them into three categories.

According to recent reports, across all three models, certain failure modes appear frequently even in runs that ultimately succeed. These are often structural frictions rather than terminal bugs.

It has been revealed that this separation is where MAST proves its value. It allows us to ignore the bening failures like repetition that often occurs in troubleshooting, and focus instead on fatal failures that killed a run.

Certain behaviors strongly separate success from failure. When these modes appear, the probability of a successful outcome drops precipitously. The most prominent example is FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification). This mode reveals a 52 percent increase in failed Gemini-3-Flash traces compared to its successful ones. Other prominent failure modes are 1.5 (Unaware of Termination Conditions) and 2.6 (Reasoning Action Mismatch).

If these happen, the run is likely dead; guiding practitioners to develop robust context management strategies across agents in the system and multiple turns of interactions.

Gemini-3-Flash is highly efficient, but its primary bottleneck is its tendency to assume success without rigorous proof. Its failure signature is dominated by a massive delta in verification errors. It often identifies the correct signals but terminates before cross-referencing them against the ground truth. To fix this, developers should implement an external verification gate. By requiring tool-based evidence like a cleared alert or a healthy metric threshold before allowing the agent to exit, we can mitigate this model’s inherent overconfidence.

While termination confusion (FM-3.1 and FM-1.5) is the prevalent failure mode for Kimi-K2, its failed trajectories are defined by a pervasive Action-Reasoning Mismatch (FM-2.6), which is present in a staggering 92% of its failures.

Kimi-K2 is a good example of an overthinking model, its reasoning chains are often too long but can fail at execution.

GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the most unstable failure signature of the cohort. This model exhibits an average of 5.3 distinct failure modes per failed trace, indicating a fundamental inability to maintain internal state.

In summary, MAST lets you split failure modes into two buckets:.

These are failures which are not fatal and from which the system can recover to successfully complete the task.

These are failures from which the system typically cannot recover.

This is the “richer understanding” piece: two models can have the same success rate on a small slice, yet fail for entirely different reasons—requiring different fixes.

It has been revealed that MAST is a tool that inspects the agentic system traces to identify fine-grain failure types that support system development and debugging. In this blog, we show that by applying MAST to ITBench, we move from generic observations ("Open models struggle") to a concrete engineering roadmap that help improving the performance of agentic systems relying on thse models, e.g.:.
