Latest Update: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Industry observers note that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Industry observers note that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," stated Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

In a recent development, for decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The upcoming findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

According to recent reports, an important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

In a recent development, producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

Recent findings suggest that to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The upcoming approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another notable discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

Industry observers note that "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler mentioned. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

Sources indicate that the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

In a recent development, the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

According to recent reports, the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems.
  • In synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections.
  • Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authors: Enzo Ruedas, Tess Boivin.

Sources indicate that recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems. First, with the integration of visual perception in Vision–Language Models (VLMs), and more recently with the generation of robot actions in Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models. Deploying these models on embedded robotic platforms remains a challenge due to tight constraints in terms of compute, memory, and power, as well as real-time control requirements.

In synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections. To tackle that, asynchronous Inference can enable smooth and continuous motion by dissociating generation from execution. However, to be effective, the end-to-end inference latency must remain shorter than the action execution duration. This temporal constraint therefore sets an upper limit on the model's throughput.

Bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution. Addressing these challenges is essential to translate recent advances in multimodal foundation models into practical and deployable embedded robotic systems.

This guide presents NXP’s hands‑on best practices for recording reliable robotic datasets, fine‑tuning VLA policies (ACT and SmolVLA), and hightlights the real-time performance that NXP i.MX 95 SoC achieves after optimization.

It has been revealed that high‑quality, consistent data beats “more but messy” data. This section turns hard‑earned lessons into concrete checklists and schemas.

In our case, we recorded a dataset for the task: "Put the tea bag in the mug.".

In a recent development, moving from scene‑only views to mixed viewpoints increases the global accuracy, but the more cameras you have the more the latency is impacted. Therefore, you must choose right compromise. In our case that balance was reached with 3 cameras:.

It has been revealed that we strongly recommend using a gripper-mounted camera. It consistently improves success rates on fine manipulation tasks by providing a close, task-relevant viewpoint. Importantly, it is also the camera that most effectively enforces correct data collection practices, allowing the operator to rely exclusively on the robot’s perception rather than observing the scene directly.

When installing a gripper camera, we recommend securing the cable with Velcro or a strain-relief guide to prevent it from obstructing the field of view or becoming disconnected during motion.

Simple hardware tweaks like heat‑shrink tubing over gripper claws increase friction, reduce roughness, reduce slippage during episodes, and increase task success rate (fewer “almost success” episodes), improving policy learning stability.

When recording a dataset, you should:.

According to recent reports, vary episodes distribution: Divide your workspace into starting-position clusters, and record at least 10 episodes per cluster. Add diversity by changing the object position and rotation.

It has been revealed that e.g. we partitioned the robot arm’s reachable workspace into 11 clusters, each measuring 10 × 10 cm.

Differentiate training & validation sets: Policies can easily overfit on the training set, so make sure that the validation set is unseen by the model.

e.g. we removed cluster 6 from the training set.

In a recent development, record the most movements you can: Small VLA models exhibit limited generalization on unseen motion. Therefore, record episodes that cover the wider ranges of degrees of freedom.

Sources indicate that e.g. we grasped the tea bag either in horizontal or vertical position.

Sources indicate that anticipate failure: Sometimes the policy will not reach the object the first time and will have to "go back to it". We noticed that having 20% of all episodes that corresponds to the case of going back to the object help the model improve overall success rate.

Recent findings suggest that e.g. around 20% of our training set corresponds to recovery episodes.

Sources indicate that this mirrors best practices across VLA papers and community guides. Here are 3 examples of data diversity within the same cluster:.

It has been revealed that starting positions 1 and 2 correspond to different positions within the same cluster. In contrast, during the recovery episode, the robot does not begin in "starting mode"; but is instead already near the mug and should proceed directly to retrieve the tea bag from that location.

In a recent development, the range providing the best trade-off between accuracy, generalization, and motion smoothness across both the training and validation sets was found for ACT (100 actions per chunk) within a 100k-160k training steps. For SMolVLA training (50 actions per chunk), the trade‑off appears after many more training steps. We found that continuing training slightly past the point where the model begins to overfit tends to improve overall accuracy.

Rule of thumb: choose final checkpoint by evaluating success on both training and validation set, not by training loss.

The i.MX 95 SoC integrates 6× Arm Cortex‑A55, a Cortex‑M7 and a Cortex M33 MCU, a Mali GPU, a new NXP ISP, and the eIQ® Neutron NPU, targeting efficient, secure edge inference with multi‑camera support and strong I/O. [nxp.com].

Instead of running the models as one monolithic graph, we decompose the VLA graph into logical stages: encoders, decoders, and action experts. Therefore, allowing each component to be optimized, scheduled, and deployed independently.

According to recent reports, this separation allows per-block optimizations. The impact of each block quantization can be measured to choose the best tradeoff between latency and accuracy. Also, isolating the action expert from the VLM was ideal to run it at lower frequency.

Sources indicate that in order to optimize the inference for i.MX 95 SoC, we explored several quantization techniques on different blocks. We found that quantizing the vision encoder and LLM prefill had limited impact on accuracy, whereas quantization of the denoising flow in the action expert significantly degrades performance.This behaviour is expected, as quantization errors are accumulating across iterative denoising steps.

That is why we decided to keep this block at higher precision to preserve stability, while on the other blocks, we explored various quantization configurations, from 8-bit mixed precision to 4-bit quantization, depending on the layers.

This increases effective control frequency, reduces observation staleness, and improves recovery behavior.

On embedded platforms such as the i.MX 95 SoC, asynchronous inference is essential — but only effective if inference latency is kept under the action horizon budget: inference time < execution time.

Our immediate objective is to improve task accuracy with SmolVLA (ONNX FP32). We have already established a baseline and measured an optimized on-board inference latency of 6.15 s.

The goal is to move from a single validated manipulation task toward a reproducible methodology for deploying VLA policies on embedded robotic systems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with over 200 merged PRs and over 50 new contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once. More robots (including our first humanoid), more policies (including the comeback of autoregressive VLAs), faster datasets, simulation environments you can load straight from the Hub, and a modernized codebase running on Python 3.12 and Transformers v5. Whether you're training policies in simulation or deploying them on real hardware, v0.5.0 has something for you.

According to recent reports, leRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), newly introduced policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes. The release also introduces EnvHub for loading simulation environments from the Hugging Face Hub, NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena integration, and a major codebase modernization with Python 3.12+, Transformers v5, and third-party policy plugins.

LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.

In a recent development, the biggest hardware addition in this release: full Unitree G1 humanoid support. This is LeRobot's first humanoid integration, and it's comprehensive:.

Recent findings suggest that the G1 integration represents a major step toward general-purpose robotics within LeRobot — moving beyond tabletop arms into full-body embodied AI. Try it out yourself by following the documentation.

It has been revealed that we've added support for the OpenArm robot and its companion OpenArm Mini teleoperator. OpenArm is a capable robot arm with full LeRobot integration, and the Mini serves as its natural teleoperation device. Both support bi-manual configurations, enabling dual-arm setups for more complex manipulation tasks. Check it out in the documentation.

The hardware ecosystem keeps growing:.

Latest motor controller support via CAN (Controller Area Network) bus opens the door to higher-performance actuators:.

These additions mean LeRobot can now drive a wider variety of professional-grade actuators beyond the existing Dynamixel and Feetech ecosystem.

This release brings six fresh policies and techniques into LeRobot, pushing the boundaries of what's possible with open-source robot learning.

Pi0-FAST brings autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models to LeRobot with FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization). Unlike the flow-matching approach of Pi0, Pi0-FAST uses an autoregressive action expert (based on Gemma 300M) that generates discretized action tokens, enabling:.

It has been revealed that real-Time Chunking is an inference-time technique from Physical Intelligence that makes flow-matching policies dramatically more responsive. Instead of waiting for a full action chunk to finish before replanning, RTC continuously blends latest predictions with in-progress actions, producing smoother and more reactive behavior.

RTC is not a standalone policy — it's an enhancement that plugs into existing flow-matching policies (Pi0 family, SmolVLA & Diffusion). Configure it via --policy.rtc_config.enabled=true.

It has been revealed that this is a game-changer for real-world deployment where latency matters. Read the original paper for the technical details and our documentation.

Sources indicate that wall-X is a new VLA policy built on Qwen2.5-VL with flow-matching action prediction. It combines the strong vision-language understanding of Qwen2.5-VL with a flow-matching head for cross-embodiment robotic control.

Industry observers note that X-VLA brings a Florence2-based VLA to LeRobot. Built on Microsoft's Florence-2 vision-language model, X-VLA offers an alternative backbone for VLA policies, expanding the diversity of foundation models available for robot learning. Check out the training guide for setup instructions and the base model.

SARM (Stage-Aware Reward Modeling) tackles one of the hardest problems in robot learning: long-horizon tasks. Instead of using a single global linear progress signal over the whole episode, it models progress in a stage-aware manner by predicting both the task stage and the progress within that stage. This makes it much easier to train policies for complex, multi-step manipulation tasks. Start experimenting with it by following the documentation.

You can now fine-tune large VLAs using LoRA (and other PEFT methods) without modifying the core training pipeline. PEFT configuration lives at the policy level, making it straightforward to adapt massive foundation models to your specific robot and task with a fraction of the compute. Learn more reading the documentation.

The dataset pipeline gets major performance improvements in this release, making both data collection and training significantly faster.

Previously, recording a dataset meant waiting after each episode for video encoding to finish. No more. With streaming video encoding, frames are encoded in real-time as they're captured — meaning zero wait time between episodes. Just finish one episode and immediately start the next.

Streaming encoding also supports hardware encoder auto-detection, so if your system has a GPU-accelerated video encoder, LeRobot will use it automatically:.

Recent findings suggest that streaming encoding performance can vary significantly depending on your hardware and recording setup (number of cameras, resolution, etc.). Make sure to review the streaming video encoding documentation before enabling it.

Under the hood, we've fixed key data access bottlenecks and overhauled image processing:.

The dataset editing toolkit continues to grow:.

Sources indicate that envHub is a new way to use simulation environments in LeRobot: load them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Instead of installing environment packages locally and wiring up registration, you can now point LeRobot at a Hub repository and it handles everything — downloading the environment code, registering it with Gymnasium, and making it available for training and evaluation.

Hub environments use HubEnvConfig, which downloads and executes remote make_env functions:.

This lowers the barrier for sharing custom simulation environments with the community. Package your environment, push it to the Hub, and anyone can train on it. Check out the documentation to learn more. Here's an example to get started: LeIsaac x LeRobot EnvHub tutorial.

Recent findings suggest that we've integrated NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, bringing GPU-accelerated simulation to LeRobot. IsaacLab-Arena provides a collection of manipulation tasks running on NVIDIA's Isaac Sim, offering massively parallel environment instances for fast reinforcement learning. The integration includes dedicated pre/post-processing steps and full compatibility with LeRobot's training pipeline. Check out the documentation.

This release modernizes the codebase:.

Beyond these headline features, v0.5.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, CI/CD enhancements, and quality-of-life improvements across the entire codebase. From better type checking to more robust test infrastructure, we're investing in the foundations that make LeRobot reliable and maintainable as it scales.

Sources indicate that we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community — contributors, consumers, and collaborators alike — for helping LeRobot grow into what it is today. Every bug report, PR, and discussion makes this project better.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Sources indicate that picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

It has been revealed that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

Sources indicate that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

It has been revealed that bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and looks auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the firm says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

It has been revealed that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Industry observers note that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising latest method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Fresh Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

It has been revealed that but quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," indicates Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

According to recent reports, rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify key interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an crucial step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

It has been revealed that looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

Sources indicate that this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

Industry observers note that the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism: Training with Million-Token Contexts

📅 09 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that training large language models on long sequences has become essential for building capable AI systems.
  • Recent findings suggest that ulysses Sequence Parallelism (part of the Arctic Long Sequence Training (ALST) protocol from Snowflake AI Research) provides an elegant solution by distributing the attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention head parallelism.
  • Recent findings suggest that the attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that training large language models on long sequences has become essential for building capable AI systems. As models are increasingly used for tasks like document analysis, code understanding, complex reasoning, and RAG workloads, the need to process sequences of hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of tokens has grown dramatically. To put this in perspective, an average book is roughly 250k tokens, so training on multi-document contexts or book-length inputs requires handling sequences well beyond what fits on a single GPU. However, training with such long contexts presents significant memory challenges: the attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length, promptly exceeding GPU memory for contexts beyond tens of thousands of tokens.

Recent findings suggest that ulysses Sequence Parallelism (part of the Arctic Long Sequence Training (ALST) protocol from Snowflake AI Research) provides an elegant solution by distributing the attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention head parallelism. In this post, we'll explore how Ulysses works and how it's been integrated across the Hugging Face ecosystem—from Accelerate to the Transformers Trainer and TRL's SFTTrainer.

Recent findings suggest that the attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length. For a sequence of length n n n, standard attention requires O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) FLOPs and O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) memory to compute and store the attention score matrix. Optimized implementations like FlashAttention reduce the memory to O(n) O(n) O(n) by tiling the computation and never materializing the full attention matrix—but the O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) compute remains. For very long sequences (32k+ tokens), even with FlashAttention, training still pushes the limits of single-GPU memory.

Consider these scenarios where long-context training is essential:.

Industry observers note that traditional data parallelism doesn't help here—each GPU still needs to process the full sequence inside the attention block. We need a way to split the sequence itself across multiple devices.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (SP), introduced in the DeepSpeed Ulysses paper, takes a clever approach: in addition to splitting on the sequence dimension, it also partitions the attention heads across GPUs.

Sequence Sharding: The input sequence is split along the sequence dimension across P P P GPUs. Each GPU i i i holds tokens [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P) [i \cdot n/P, (i+1) \cdot n/P) [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P).

QKV Projection: Each GPU computes the query, key, and value projections for its local sequence chunk.

All-to-All Communication: An all-to-all collective operation redistributes the data so that each GPU holds all sequence positions after the projections, but only for a subset of attention heads.

Local Attention: Each GPU computes attention for its assigned heads using standard attention mechanisms (FlashAttention or SDPA).

All-to-All Communication: Another all-to-all operation reverses the redistribution, returning to sequence-sharded format.

Output Projection: Each GPU computes the output projection for its local sequence chunk.

The key insight is that attention heads are independent—each head can be computed separately. By trading sequence locality for head locality, Ulysses enables efficient parallelization with relatively low communication overhead.

Ulysses requires two all-to-all operations per attention layer, with total communication volume of O(n⋅d/P) O(n \cdot d / P) O(n⋅d/P) per GPU, where:.

Ring Attention communicates O(n⋅d) O(n \cdot d) O(n⋅d) per GPU — a factor of P P P more — via P−1 P-1 P−1 sequential point-to-point transfers around the ring. Ulysses also benefits from lower latency because all-to-all can exploit full bisectional bandwidth in a single collective step, whereas Ring Attention serializes over P−1 P-1 P−1 hops.

Accelerate provides the foundation for Ulysses sequence parallelism through its ParallelismConfig class and DeepSpeed integration.

When you call accelerator.prepare(), Ulysses is automatically set up:.

With Ulysses, each GPU computes loss on different parts of the sequence. The losses must be aggregated properly, weighted by the number of valid tokens per rank. If you're using the Transformers Trainer or TRL's SFTTrainer, this is handled automatically—the code below is only needed when writing a custom Accelerate training loop:.

The weighted loss aggregation ensures correct gradients when tokens are unevenly distributed across ranks (e.g., when some ranks contain only padding or masked out prompt tokens).

Both Ulysses and Ring Attention use position_ids instead of attention_mask for causal masking during training. A 4D attention mask at these sequence lengths would be just as prohibitive as the attention scores themselves—at 128k tokens, that's another ~1TB tensor. Position IDs achieve the same causal behavior with O(n) O(n) O(n) memory instead of O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2). During evaluation/inference, DeepSpeed's SP attention layer can bypass the SP operations entirely (via disable_in_eval) and fall back to the model's default attention implementation.

In a recent development, the Transformers Trainer provides seamless Ulysses integration through TrainingArguments.parallelism_config. It handles all the SP-specific details automatically—dataloader wrapping, sequence sharding, and loss aggregation—so you don't need to write any of the custom loss code shown above.

Just pass the same parallelism_config from above into TrainingArguments:.

Dataloader Wrapping: After model preparation, the Trainer wraps the dataloader with UlyssesSPDataLoaderAdapter.

Batch Size Calculation: The effective data parallel world size accounts for SP:.

Dataloader Length Adjustment: Training step calculations are adjusted for SP's effect on iteration count.

The SFTTrainer automatically handles pre-shifted labels when Ulysses is enabled:.

Both Ulysses and Ring Attention enable long-context training, but they have different characteristics:.

Since switching between the two only requires changing the accelerate config, we recommend trying both and comparing performance and memory usage on your specific setup. The main constraint is that Ulysses requires num_heads >= sp_size, while Ring Attention has no such limitation.

If your desired model architecture is supported by Liger-Kernel, it is fully compatible with Ulysses SP and can be enabled with a single flag:.

The main memory saving comes from FusedLinearCrossEntropy which avoids materializing the full logits tensor during loss calculation. The savings grow with longer sequences where the logits tensor is larger.

Additionally, you can enable TiledMLP to further extend sequence length — like FusedLinearCrossEntropy, it saves working memory by tiling large matrix operations.

You don't need to worry about manually balancing tokens across SP ranks—the loss aggregation code handles uneven distributions gracefully (including ranks with zero valid tokens). With random batching over a reasonably sized dataset, the distribution evens out statistically over training.

To quantify the benefits of Ulysses SP, we trained Qwen3-4B on the Gutenberg English streaming dataset using TRL's SFTTrainer. All experiments ran on H100 80GB GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, CPU optimizer offloading, gradient checkpointing, and flash-attn2 as the attention backend.

The benchmark runs in the table above use the same global batch size (8 micro-batches), cosine learning-rate schedule, and seed, so those benchmark loss curves are directly comparable.

To verify SP-vs-DP loss equivalence, we ran controlled 4-GPU A/B experiments with identical seed, model, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and data order.

For fair comparison, GAS must scale with SP:.

Measured over 20 steps on 4 GPUs in controlled equivalence harnesses:.

Industry observers note that takeaway: under matched token budget, SP and non-SP match on canonical token-normalized loss. The remaining difference is in trainer-reported logging (loss), not in the underlying cross-entropy objective.

It has been revealed that at 8K tokens, DP=4 and SP=4 use nearly the same memory per GPU (~22 GB with ZeRO-3). The advantage of SP is that it enables scaling to much longer sequences: at 96K tokens (12x longer), peak memory is 66 GB — still within the H100's 80 GB capacity. At 128K, the model OOMs, establishing the practical limit for this configuration. DP=4 without SP cannot scale beyond 8K for this model.

At the same sequence length (8K), SP=4 has comparable throughput to the single-GPU baseline — the all-to-all communication overhead is minimal on NVLink-connected GPUs. The real benefit comes from longer sequences: as sequence length grows, the quadratic attention computation dominates over communication and other overheads, making each training step increasingly compute-efficient. Each step also processes proportionally more tokens, so throughput scales with sequence length. At 64K, SP=4 processes 13,396 tokens/second — 3.7x the baseline.

These results use only 4 GPUs with SP=4. With 8 GPUs (SP=8), you can push to even longer sequences — up to 256K+ tokens — or use 2D parallelism (SP=4, DP=2) to combine long-context training with data-parallel throughput.

In a recent development, use flash_attention_2 for Ampere GPUs, or flash_attention_3 for Hopper GPUs. Wait for flash_attention_4 on Blackwell 🕰.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest enhancement from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

Industry observers note that so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

According to recent reports, today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

According to recent reports, A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Sources indicate that another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice swiftly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows rapidly.

In a recent development, the safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

An expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

Industry observers note that the damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

Recent findings suggest that nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

Look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

In a recent development, what closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

Industry observers note that for each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the problem date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

Keep the Tokens Flowing: Lessons from 16 Open-Source RL Libraries

📅 10 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR -- For those of you who don't have time to read 5,000 words about async RL plumbing (we get it, you have models to train):.
  • If you'd rather skip straight to the good part, here's the full comparison table (no reading required, we won't judge).
