Latest Update: OlmoEarth v1.1: A more efficient family of Earth observation models

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.
  • We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025.
  • When OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.

We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025. Since then, partners have applied it across a wide range of tasks, from tracking mangrove change to classifying drivers of forest loss to producing country-scale crop-type maps in days, scaling deployments to national, continental, and global areas. Every release moves us closer to our mission: bringing state-of-the-art AI to organizations and communities working to protect people and our planet.

When OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible. Over the full lifecycle of running OlmoEarth – data export, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing – compute is by far the highest cost. A more efficient model means we can support more partners on the OlmoEarth Platform, and that anyone running OlmoEarth on their own can leverage this technology faster and at lower expense.

That’s why we built OlmoEarth v1.1: a fresh family of models that cuts compute costs by up to 3x while maintaining OlmoEarth v1's performance on a mix of research benchmarks and tasks we’ve constructed with partners.

Industry observers note that the OlmoEarth models are transformer-based models, one of the dominant architectures in machine learning today. To process remote sensing data, we first convert it into a sequence of tokens the model can ingest.

Two important levers control efficiency in transformer-based models: model size (this is why we release a family of models, so users can pick the size that fits their compute budget) and token sequence length. Compute costs scale quadratically with the token sequence length, so even small reductions can meaningfully cut the cost of running the model.

Industry observers note that MACs, or multiply-accumulate operations, estimate the computation needed for one model forward pass; lower MACs generally mean cheaper, faster inference. The y-axis is inverted because lower average rank is better. Labels show model family and size. All plotted points use the pasted MAC/rank values.

This raises an key question for transformer-based remote sensing models: what should a token represent?

In a recent development, take Sentinel-2 imagery, a common modality we process. A Sentinel-2 input will be some tensor with a height and width (H, W representing the latitudinal and longitudinal pixels), a temporal dimension T, and 12 Sentinel-2 channels ([H, W, T, D=12]).

At the moment, we split the data into resolution-based patches. Concretely, this means that we will pick some spatial patch size p, and split our overall Sentinel-2 image into patches of size p x p:.

For each patch, we create a token per timestep per resolution. So a Sentinel-2 input with 2 timesteps yields 6 tokens per patch (2 timesteps x 3 resolutions, 10m, 20m, and 60m).

In total, a[H, W, T, D=12] Sentinel-2 input will yield H/p x W/p x T x 3 tokens.

Using a unique token per resolution is a common technique when processing Sentinel-2 data—Galileo and SatMAE both take this approach, and SatMAE shows significantly better results when doing it. However, it is not universal: CROMA is a model that only uses a single token for all bands, regardless of resolution. Because token counts compound multiplicatively, collapsing resolutions into a single token produces three times fewer tokens and material savings across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference.

Recent findings suggest that naively combining the tokens in this way leads to significant performance drops, including a 10 ppt drop on m-eurosat kNN (a common benchmark task for remote sensing models). We hypothesize that separating Sentinel-2 bands into different tokens makes it easier for OlmoEarth to model important cross-band relationships.

Merging tokens without impacting performance required us to modify our pre-training regimen. We describe those changes in detail in our paper.

Industry observers note that the result is a model family that does more with less. At every size, OlmoEarth v1.1 runs up to three times cheaper than OlmoEarth v1, making frequent, planet-scale map refreshes more affordable for every team running OlmoEarth. If you're using a model from the original OlmoEarth family, try OlmoEarth v1.1. It provides similar performance to OlmoEarth v1 while requiring one third of the compute, though we have seen some regressions (see our technical report for more details). If it works for your task, you should see a significant speedup during fine-tuning and inference.

Pretrained remote sensing models have many degrees of freedom, which makes them hard to study. When performance shifts, is it the architecture, the dataset, or the pre-training algorithm?

We train OlmoEarth v1.1 on the same dataset as OlmoEarth v1, so any differences between the two isolate the effect of methodological changes. We hope this advances understanding of scientific principles when pretraining models for remote sensing.

Check out the OlmoEarth v1.1 weights and training code, including the weights for our Base, Tiny, and Nano models.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why RAG If You Already Have a Database? Explained Simply 🔎

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your company already keeps its HR policies in a database.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post explains why that happens, what RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) adds on top of your database, and when you don't need it at all.
  • A database is a very fast, very literal librarian.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your company already keeps its HR policies in a database. An employee types: "Can I carry over my unused holidays to next year?" The answer is sitting right there in a table, and the search box still returns nothing useful.

Recent findings suggest that this post explains why that happens, what RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) adds on top of your database, and when you don't need it at all. You'll see a small before-and-after in Python.

A database is a very fast, very literal librarian. Ask for the book with ID 4021 and you get it instantly. Ask for "rows where the text contains carry over" and it checks every row for those exact letters. If the policy says "rolled forward" instead, the librarian shrugs. It isn't being lazy; it was never built to understand language.

Here is our running example. The table holds four policy lines:.

The employee says "carry over" and "holidays". The policy says "rolled forward" and "annual leave". Same meaning, zero shared words. Worse, the word "holidays" does appear, but in the wrong row (public holidays).

It has been revealed that you might say: "Postgres has full-text search." It helps. Postgres can reduce words to a base form, so rats matches rat, and it can rank results by relevance. But matching "carry over" to "rolled forward" needs a synonym dictionary that someone writes and maintains by hand. Nobody can list every way a person might phrase a question.

That gap is what RAG fills. Three terms first:.

RAG = Retrieve the most relevant text by meaning, Augment (add) it to the question, and let the LLM Generate an answer from it. The idea was introduced in a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research. Their main point still holds: a model's built-in knowledge is hard to upgrade and hard to check, while text you fetch from a store can be updated any time and shown as evidence.

Notice the database is still there on the left. RAG changes how you search it and adds a reader at the end.

Sources indicate that you keep your policy lines as before. Next to each one, you also save its embedding. This happens once, when a policy is added or changed, not on every question. The numbers can live in a dedicated vector database or in the database you already run (Postgres with the pgvector extension, for example).

When a question arrives, you turn it into an embedding using the same model, then pick the stored lines whose numbers are closest. "Carry over my unused holidays" lands near "unused annual leave rolled forward", because the model learned from huge amounts of text that these phrases are used the same way.

According to recent reports, the retrieved lines still aren't an answer; they're evidence. You pass them to an LLM with an instruction like "answer using only this text, and say you don't know if it isn't covered." The employee gets: "Yes, up to 5 days of unused annual leave can roll into next year.".

Before: plain SQL. This runs as-is with Python's built-in sqlite3.

One search finds nothing. The other finds the wrong policy. The database did exactly what it was told.

In a recent development, after: RAG. It uses sentence-transformers for free local embeddings and the Anthropic SDK for the LLM (you need an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).

In a recent development, the two things to compare: the WHERE text LIKE line became model.similarity(...), and a new step hands the result to an LLM. Your data didn't change. Only the way you search it and present it did.

Industry observers note that here's the honest part. "The database can't solve it, AI can" is true only for a specific kind of question.

Recent findings suggest that A good rule: if the question has an exact answer in a column, use SQL. If the answer is buried in sentences and people will phrase it their own way, consider RAG.

Your database stores the answer; RAG helps someone find and read it when they don't know your exact wording. It doesn't replace the database, it sits on top of it. Next step: run the "after" script, then ask it something your policies don't cover (like "Is there a pet insurance strategy?") and check that it says it doesn't know.

What's a question your owners ask that your current search box can't handle? Tell me in the comments 👇.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, altaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its new 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).

AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them presently placed in its offices and clinics.

In a recent development, “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), said in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”.

According to recent reports, in recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.

Patssi Valdez and rafa esparza’s Sacred and Profane Beauty (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

Industry observers note that “The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”.

Recent findings suggest that some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.

AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.

The artist Felicia Montes at La Botánica del Barrio (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

In a recent development, the first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.

She indicates she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.

It has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she states. The company has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.

Down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".

Industry observers note that the other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

Tech Report: What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S.
  • “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy.
  • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

It has been revealed that urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Recent findings suggest that working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” stated Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

According to recent reports, natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin noted.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who mentioned they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” remarked Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy mentioned tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related complications than average.

In a recent development, another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

Sources indicate that “I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” remarked Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Sources indicate that fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio stated. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

Sources indicate that this article was originally published on Stanford News. Read the original article.

Melissa De Witte is the deputy director for social science communications for the Stanford News Service. She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

#103566. Latest Update: Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right

📅 25 May 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2235 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right

📅 25 May 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when a field evolves rapidly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding.
  • It has been revealed that this can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments.
  • Industry observers note that "What do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when a field evolves rapidly, its vocabulary often evolves faster than its shared understanding. Terms start to blur, get reused in different contexts, or become shorthand for ideas that are never fully explained. We are currently seeing this happen in the field of AI Agents, where concepts are getting mixed together, some are renamed, and others are widely used for a few months before quietly disappearing.

It has been revealed that this can be overwhelming for newcomers, and even for practitioners trying to keep up with the latest developments. After ICLR 2026, one of us (@ariG23498) posted a question that captured this confusion well:.

Industry observers note that "What do you mean by the terms 'harness' and 'scaffold' in the context of agents? I have heard a lot of explanations while I was at ICLR, but I could not understand why they did not converge to a single explanation.".

This glossary is our attempt to ground the terms that keep coming up without clear, consistent explanations. It is not meant to be a comprehensive dictionary of every term in the field. Instead, we focus on the concepts that are often mixed up, reused in different ways, or assumed to be obvious when they are not.

Most of these terms come up whether you're building an agent, deploying one, or just using tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Hermes Agent. The last section covers concepts specific to training models, which is more relevant if you work on that side of things.

It has been revealed that many of these terms don't have universally accepted definitions yet, and different frameworks use the same word differently. The goal here is not to enforce one correct vocabulary, but to provide a practical mental model that makes discussions easier to follow.

Sources indicate that the model is the LLM: it takes text in and produces text out (e.g., Claude, Qwen, GPT, Kimi, DeepSeek…). On its own, it has no memory between calls, and no loop. The model can express the intent to call a tool, but it needs a harness to actually execute it. It answers one prompt and stops. Wrap it in scaffolding and a harness and it becomes an agent.

Industry observers note that the behavior-defining layer around the model: system prompt, tool descriptions, how the model's responses get parsed, what it remembers across steps (context management). It shapes how the model sees the world and acts in it, whether during training or at inference.

Products like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity CLI call the whole thing a harness. Claude Code's own docs say it directly: "Claude Code serves as the agentic harness around Claude." That's the broad use: harness means everything that isn't the model. The scaffold/harness distinction matters most when you need to reason about them separately, as in a training pipeline. You'll also hear "scaffold" used more broadly to cover any infrastructure the harness relies on: hooks, runtime configuration, even directory structure.

Some products like Claude Code and Codex are tightly coupled to their provider's models. Others like Antigravity CLI and Hermes Agent let you plug in any model.

The execution layer inside the agent: it calls the model, handles its tool calls, decides when to stop. The harness is what makes the agent run. Scaffolding, defined above, is what the model works from: its instructions, its tools, its format.

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing this layer well: deciding when the agent should stop, how errors get handled, and what guardrails keep it on track. It applies at both training and inference. Addy Osmani's piece and OpenAI's account of building with Codex both cover this from the inference side.

At evaluation time, the same pattern indicates up as an eval harness: instead of collecting training data, it runs a fixed set of scenarios at a model checkpoint and records metrics rather than updating weights.

Some frameworks use orchestrator for a higher-level controller that coordinates work across multiple agents. Unlike a harness, which drives a model through its execution loop, an orchestrator manages agents as units, each running their own harness (see Sub-agents below).

Recent findings suggest that the term comes from reinforcement learning, where an agent is simply a function that takes an observation and returns an action. The environment takes that action and returns a fresh observation, and the loop repeats. That loop is still at the core of how LLM agents work.

According to recent reports, in the LLM world, the term has expanded. An agent is a model plus everything around it that lets it act, not just respond. It turns raw text generation into something that can act in a loop: taking in information, deciding what to do, and acting on the results.

In a recent development, take a coding agent as a concrete example. The system prompt, tool descriptions, and the output format the model follows form the scaffolding. The loop that calls the model, handles its tool calls, and decides when to stop is the harness. At training time, the harness also runs many of these loops in parallel and feeds the results back to patch the model.

Recent findings suggest that in the community, it's usually put as Agent = Model + Harness (@Vtrivedy10 and Will Brown's tweet for reference). If you're not the model, you're the harness. The subtle distinction between harness and scaffold that creates most of the confusion is what the two sections above address.

When people talk about products like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, they're referring to a specific harness built on top of a specific model, designed and optimized together. Two products using the same underlying model can feel completely different because their harnesses make different choices. And swapping a better model into the same harness also changes the experience. The model, the harness, and the product are three different things.

Recent findings suggest that designing what goes into the agent's context window: what the model sees at each step, system prompt, tool descriptions, conversation history, retrieved knowledge. It's not a one-time decision: as the model runs, previous turns shape what goes into future calls, and the harness actively manages this throughout the run. It applies at both training and inference, but the cost of getting it wrong is very different. At training, what the model sees shapes what gets learned. Get it wrong and you're retraining. At inference, it's just text: change a prompt and redeploy. The HF Context Engineering Course covers this in depth.

Memory is part of this picture. Short-term memory is what stays in the context window during a single run: conversation history, tool results, previous reasoning. Long-term memory persists across sessions, stored externally and retrieved on demand, then injected back into context when relevant.

Industry observers note that A policy is the behavior an agent follows: given any situation, it defines the probability of taking each possible action. In LLM systems, part of that policy is learned in the model weights, but the behavior also depends on the surrounding scaffolding and harness. The same model can behave very differently depending on its prompts, tools, memory, and execution loop.

Sources indicate that A policy is not an agent. The policy defines behavior; the agent is the full system that acts in an environment. Wrap a checkpoint in scaffolding and a harness and deploy it, and you get an agent whose behavior is the policy.

According to recent reports, how agents reach outside themselves: APIs, code interpreters, databases, web search, file systems. The model expresses the intent to use a tool in a structured format. Modern inference APIs surface this as a first-class object: the harness receives the call directly and routes it to the right function. The result gets fed back into context and the loop continues.

According to recent reports, reusable, structured packages of knowledge that enable multi-step tasks. Where a tool is an action ("run this command"), a skill bundles everything needed to accomplish a goal ("investigate this bug, form a hypothesis, write a fix"). They are portable across agents and loaded on demand. The line between tool, skill, and sub-agent shifts across frameworks. The HF Context Engineering Course covers skills in depth.

An agent called by another agent to handle a specific subtask. It has its own model and scaffold, reasons independently, and returns a result. The calling agent doesn't need to know how it works internally. This is what separates a sub-agent from a tool (a function call) or a skill (packaged knowledge): a sub-agent can itself reason, use tools, and call further sub-agents. The calling agent is sometimes called an orchestrator.

The terms above apply whether you're training or deploying. These four are specific to training, where the agent runs through tasks, gets scored, and its model's weights get updated. Every RL training system for LLMs is built around the same pipeline:.

The environment is anything you can interact with: a stateful object that takes an action as input, updates its internal state, and returns an observation. In the LLM context, actions are typically tool calls. A filesystem is a simple example: the action touch foo.txt updates the state by creating the file, and the observation might be the updated file listing. Definitions vary across frameworks.

We recently published a dedicated guide on this, so rather than compress it here, see The Ultimate Guide to RL Environments for a complete breakdown of types, frameworks, and examples.

Sources indicate that the trainer is what makes the agent better: it runs many agent episodes, scores the results and uses them to update the inner model's weights. TRL's GRPOTrainer is a concrete example: a single class that handles episode generation, reward scoring, and weight updates.

It has been revealed that A rollout is one full agent run from start to finish: what the agent saw, what it did, and what reward it got at each step. It's also called a trajectory or a trace, depending on the context. This is the raw data RL algorithms learn from.

Industry observers note that the score that tells the training algorithm whether the model is getting better. It can be verifiable (tests pass/fail, answer matches), or learned (human preferences, LLM-as-judge), sparse (one score at the end of an episode), or dense (a score at each step). This is what the trainer uses to actually patch the inner model's weights. For a thorough breakdown of each type, see the Reward Architecture section in Adithya's guide.

In a recent development, rubrics break the reward into explicit dimensions with weights, rather than a single number. OpenEnv and Verifiers implement rubrics as objects you can combine (WeightedSum, Sequential, Gate).

If any definition feels imprecise or you've encountered a term we've missed, we'd love to hear from you.

Thanks to Pedro Cuenca, Quentin Gallouédec, Shaun Smith, and Adithya S Kolavi for reviewing this post.

The definition of Agent in popular use changes every year :).

We really leaned into Autonomy in this post from last year, but this year it seems to be all about model + harnesses: https://huggingface.co/blog/ethics-soc-7.

All in all, the more precise and technically specific the term, the better!

It has been revealed that coding Agent, or Agent CLI – a command-line application, used to launch and manage agent instances (e.g. Opencode, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, etc).

Agent Definition – a file (Markdown/JSON) that describes how an agent behaves; serves as a blueprint from which instances are created (like a class in Java).

Agent Instance – a running process created from an Agent Definition (like an object instantiated from a class in Java).

Agent / AI Agent – avoid; use the specific term (CLI, Definition, or Instance) depending on what you mean; not to forget that “Agent” can also mean the CI pipeline agent or a human agent.

Where do MCPs fit in all of this?

Recent findings suggest that it's a standardization protocol that makes the Tool Use → Harness connection much cleaner and more interoperable. The glossary describes what agents do; MCP is a specification for how they do the tool-calling part reliably across different vendors and implementations.

According to recent reports, appreciate the nice writeup. Can we add a) Leaderboard, b) Benchmark.

https://github.com/IBM/AssetOpsBench.

Really useful glossary, and I especially appreciate the attempt to separate the model, harness, scaffold, tools, context, and training loop.

One concern I have is with standardizing on “scaffolding” as the term for the behavior-defining layer around the model. To me, “scaffolding” already feels quite overloaded, specifically in software projects. It is used extensively in code generation, and more narrowly by framework generators to create routes, controllers, models, migrations, components, tests, and other boilerplate structures.

I wonder whether “rigging” might be a better candidate. It still relates naturally to the metaphor of a harness, but is less already-standardized in adjacent software and AI contexts. In the horse/cart sense, rigging is the arrangement that attaches the harness to the thing being pulled and makes the whole setup usable. That feels close to what this layer does for an agent: system prompt, tool descriptions, response formats, memory/context rules, and other configurations that connect the model to the operational environment in a particular way.

This is the best article I read so far on this topic, thank you for sharing this, now at least I can better understand how to learn more about AI Agents. Ty!

Breaking: Why AI Voice Agents Are Becoming a Hot Investment in Healthcare

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technical breakdown of real-time voice processing, automated appointment scheduling, patient data security, and the engineering challenges behind production-ready healthcare AI agents.
  • Building an AI voice agent that answers a phone call is relatively straightforward.
  • Building one that can understand a patient, check a doctor's availability, book an appointment, enhancement the hospital's system, and handle unexpected situations without compromising patient safety is a completely different engineering problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical breakdown of real-time voice processing, automated appointment scheduling, patient data security, and the engineering challenges behind production-ready healthcare AI agents.

Building an AI voice agent that answers a phone call is relatively straightforward.

Building one that can understand a patient, check a doctor's availability, book an appointment, enhancement the hospital's system, and handle unexpected situations without compromising patient safety is a completely different engineering problem.

According to Invoca's 2026 Healthcare Lead Conversion Benchmarks, only 54% of healthcare calls are answered by a person.

In a recent development, that doesn't mean every remaining caller is lost. Some calls may reach automated systems or voicemail. But it highlights a significant opportunity for improving how healthcare organizations handle incoming calls.

This is one reason healthcare-focused voice AI platforms are attracting attention.

Companies like Assort Health, Prosper AI, and Hippocratic AI are exploring different applications, from appointment scheduling and patient administration to post-discharge follow-ups.

For developers, however, the interesting part isn't how naturally these systems can speak.

It's how they work behind the conversation.

A reliable healthcare voice agent requires real-time audio streaming, speech recognition, conversation management, secure integrations, deterministic workflows, and carefully designed human escalation.

Let's break down how we can approach building such a system.

The architecture and code examples in this article are illustrative implementation patterns, not the internal implementations of the companies mentioned.

A traditional chatbot follows a relatively simple request-response model.

The user types a message, the application sends it to an AI model, and the model generates a response.

Voice applications introduce several additional problems.

It has been revealed that the system must handle streaming audio while keeping the conversation responsive. Patients may speak over the agent, change their requests halfway through a sentence, or provide incomplete information.

Patient: "I'd like to see Dr. Smith tomorrow morning.".

Agent: "I found an appointment at 10:30 AM.".

Patient: "Actually, could you make that Friday? And I need to check if my insurance covers it.".

The agent now needs to maintain conversational state, enhancement the scheduling request, retrieve new availability, and possibly initiate an insurance eligibility workflow.

Generating a natural-language response is only one part of that process.

Each component addresses a different engineering responsibility.

The telephony layer establishes the call.

The speech recognition layer converts audio into text.

The conversation engine determines what the patient is trying to accomplish.

The orchestration layer executes approved actions through backend services.

Finally, text-to-speech (TTS) converts the response into audio.

The vital design principle is to separate conversation generation from operational execution.

The AI model can interpret patient requests, but backend services should control what actions are actually permitted.

One of the first architectural decisions involves handling audio.

There are two common approaches.

This pipeline gives developers explicit access to transcribed text, which can help with structured intent extraction and debugging.

However, each processing stage introduces latency.

An alternative is a real-time multimodal model capable of receiving and generating audio directly.

This can simplify parts of the pipeline and potentially improve conversational responsiveness.

However, the application still needs a separate layer for tool authorization, workflow validation, auditability, and safety controls.

Recent findings suggest that in healthcare, a natural-sounding conversation is not enough. The system must produce operationally correct outcomes.

A telephony platform such as Twilio can stream call audio to an application using WebSockets.

For example, Twilio supports bidirectional Media Streams through its mechanism.

A simplified connection configuration looks like this:.

The application receives audio events over the WebSocket connection and sends supported audio messages back for playback.

Twilio's Media Streams documentation describes the underlying streaming capabilities.

A production implementation also needs to validate incoming connections, support the provider's audio protocol, manage active sessions, and recover from stream interruptions.

Latency has a direct impact on user experience.

If the agent takes several seconds to answer every question, the call quickly becomes frustrating.

Engineers should measure several separate components:.

Instead of optimizing only average latency, measure p95 and p99 response times.

It's also important to support barge-in, where the caller interrupts the agent while it is speaking.

When that happens, the system may need to stop outgoing audio, cancel a pending response, and process the latest input without losing the current conversation context.

This is one reason voice applications require more careful state management than ordinary text chatbots.

A common approach when building early AI agents is to send the entire conversation history to an LLM and ask it what to do next.

But healthcare workflows should not rely entirely on a language model remembering which steps have been completed.

Consider an appointment scheduling flow.

The application should track these steps explicitly.

A simple TypeScript state model might look like:.

The LLM can help interpret the patient's language and propose the next action.

But a workflow controller should validate whether the requested transition is permitted.

These rules belong in application logic, not just in a system prompt.

Sources indicate that use the LLM for understanding language. Use deterministic code for enforcing workflow rules.

This is where healthcare voice AI becomes significantly more complex than a general-purpose customer support bot.

A voice agent isn't particularly useful if it can only tell a patient:.

"Someone from the clinic will call you back to complete your appointment.".

The real operational value comes from connecting the conversation to the clinic's existing systems.

Healthcare organizations may use platforms such as Epic, Oracle Health/Cerner, or athenahealth.

But these systems don't all expose identical APIs or permit the same operations.

FHIR, or Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, provides standardized resources for exchanging healthcare information.

For scheduling-related workflows, relevant resources can include:.

These resources are defined in the HL7 FHIR specification.

FHIR provides a common data model, but it does not guarantee that every EHR supports appointment booking through a public write API.

In practice, scheduling integration may require proprietary APIs, HL7 interfaces, vendor-specific workflows, or integrations through a practice management system.

Instead of allowing the AI agent to communicate directly with each EHR, create an integration boundary.

The conversation engine should call an internal operation such as:.

The adapter handles the vendor-specific integration.

This also helps isolate business rules from external APIs.

Imagine the patient confirms a booking, but the network connection times out.

The agent doesn't know whether the hospital system completed the operation.

If it simply retries, the patient could receive two appointments.

The booking layer should use an idempotency key and implement duplicate protection wherever the underlying system supports it.

If the EHR doesn't provide idempotent booking operations, the adapter needs a reconciliation strategy.

Industry observers note that this is intentionally simplified. A production workflow also needs authorization, durable request tracking, concurrency control, timeout handling, and verification of ambiguous booking results.

The crucial point is that a successful conversation is not the same thing as a successful database operation.

Never tell a patient that an appointment is confirmed until the authoritative scheduling system establishes that result.

Insurance eligibility is another valuable use case for healthcare voice agents.

But it introduces additional complexity.

The patient may provide a payer name, member ID, and other identifying details.

The application must validate those details before submitting an eligibility request to an authorized payer integration.

A simplified flow looks like this:.

An important distinction is that insurance eligibility does not necessarily guarantee payment or establish an exact final patient responsibility.

Coverage can depend on plan terms, service type, deductibles, authorization requirements, and claim processing.

Therefore, a voice agent should not generate an exact copay merely because a language model thinks one is likely.

It should only communicate values supported by an authoritative response, with appropriate qualifications.

When eligibility information is unavailable or uncertain, the workflow should route the issue to billing staff rather than invent an answer.

This is a recurring principle in healthcare AI development:.

The model can explain verified information, but it should not manufacture operational facts.

Healthcare voice agents may process protected health information (PHI), including patient names, appointment details, symptoms, insurance information, and other sensitive data.

That makes privacy and security foundational system requirements.

HIPAA compliance is not achieved simply by enabling encryption or using a cloud provider that advertises healthcare support.

The applicable requirements depend on the organization, its role, its vendors, and how PHI is processed.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services explains that cloud service providers handling electronic PHI on behalf of covered entities or business associates generally require appropriate Business Associate Agreements (BAAs).

That matters because a healthcare voice application can involve multiple vendors.

Each component needs to be reviewed for its role in receiving, transmitting, storing, or processing PHI.

A suitable architecture should account for several safeguards.

Protect data in transit and at rest using appropriate security controls.

Encryption is important, but it is only one part of a broader security program.

Use role-based authorization, narrowly scoped credentials, and appropriate patient identity verification.

A call originating from a patient's known phone number should not automatically be treated as proof of identity.

Not every conversation requires permanent audio recording or full transcript retention.

Consider whether the workflow can operate with structured outcomes such as:.

This record intentionally avoids patient details, but other session data and associated identifiers may still be regulated or sensitive.

If audio or transcripts need to be retained, define access controls, retention periods, deletion policies, and permitted uses.

Debug logs can easily become an unexpected repository of PHI.

Avoid recording raw transcripts, authentication tokens, insurance member IDs, or medical details in ordinary application logs.

Use structured operational events and carefully controlled audit records instead.

Sending a confirmation SMS may be useful, but the message content and delivery mechanism should follow the healthcare organization's communication policies, patient preferences, and applicable privacy requirements.

Redaction can reduce exposure, but it does not automatically make a system HIPAA compliant.

Privacy controls need to cover the entire data lifecycle, not only what reaches the database.

Not every patient request should be completed by an AI agent.

This is especially key in healthcare.

A patient may begin a call by asking for an appointment and then mention symptoms suggesting an urgent medical situation.

The system needs a way to interrupt normal workflows and initiate an approved escalation process.

A basic safety layer might look like this:.

This code illustrates the routing boundary, not a clinically validated emergency detector.

A production system needs clinician-approved protocols, tested detection methods, conservative escalation rules, and monitoring for missed high-risk situations.

Keyword matching alone is inadequate, and an LLM classifier should not be treated as a reliable medical triage system without rigorous validation.

Recent findings suggest that for a U.S. healthcare deployment, an emergency protocol might direct someone with a potentially life-threatening emergency to contact 911 immediately.

The precise language and workflow should be established with the healthcare organization.

A voice agent should not attempt to diagnose the patient or provide unsupported reassurance while deciding whether to escalate.

This is an vital failure scenario.

A clinic may not have an available nurse at midnight.

A transfer could fail because the destination number is busy or unavailable.

The system needs predefined fallback behavior rather than repeatedly attempting transfers while the patient waits.

Possible fallback actions include an approved emergency instruction, an alternate staffed line, or a documented callback workflow for non-emergency cases.

Escalation isn't just a conversational feature.

It's an operational system that needs its own reliability testing.

Voice agents depend on several services working together.

A successful call might involve the telephony provider, streaming connection, speech model, conversation model, EHR API, and messaging provider.

Each dependency introduces failure scenarios.

For non-critical processing, background queues can improve system resilience.

Examples include sending confirmation messages, generating operational analytics, and performing post-call reporting.

However, not everything should be asynchronous.

The appointment booking outcome must be established before the agent promises the patient a confirmed appointment.

Notifications can happen later.

This distinction separates the critical transaction path from supporting background work.

The core patient workflow should not depend on unrelated analytics services being available.

Traditional AI benchmarks focus on model quality, reasoning ability, and language understanding.

A healthcare voice agent needs operational metrics as well.

A system may sound convincing but still fail to book appointments correctly.

That's why production monitoring should cover several categories.

One common metric is the containment rate, or the percentage of calls completed without human assistance.

But higher containment is not always better.

A healthcare agent that correctly transfers a concerning call to a nurse may be performing exactly as intended.

A system that keeps the caller engaged with AI instead of escalating could produce a higher containment rate while providing a less safe service.

For this reason, quality and safety should be evaluated alongside automation rates.

Before a pilot, create a controlled test suite using synthetic patient data.

Run these tests against the complete call workflow, not only the LLM.

That includes streaming audio, backend tools, error handling, and actual integration responses in an appropriately isolated test environment.

A common development mistake is attempting to automate every front-desk workflow immediately.

Scheduling, insurance verification, billing, referrals, clinical inquiries, and outbound follow-up calls all have different dependencies and risk profiles.

A more practical MVP can be introduced in phases.

Start with low-risk administrative capabilities:.

This phase helps validate telephony reliability, transcription quality, and conversational experience.

Introduce a controlled scheduling integration.

Start with a limited set of appointment types and providers.

Add patient verification, availability lookup, explicit confirmation, duplicate prevention, and reliable booking outcomes.

Once the foundational system is stable, expand to capabilities such as:.

These features should be introduced only after the relevant integrations, permissions, operational policies, and exception handling are ready.

This incremental approach makes it easier to measure actual value without exposing patients and staff to unnecessary complexity.

The most useful way to think about healthcare voice AI is not as a replacement for a receptionist.

It's as a conversational interface to a collection of controlled healthcare workflows.

The language model is responsible for understanding natural speech and communicating clearly.

The application backend is responsible for identity verification, authorization, workflow state, and tool execution.

The EHR or practice management system remains the authoritative source for patient and appointment information.

Human staff remain responsible for decisions that require professional judgment, clinical expertise, or escalation.

That separation creates a much more dependable architecture.

At EnactOn, this is the architectural perspective we bring to AI-powered workflow automation: connect intelligent interfaces to dependable systems, rather than treating the language model itself as the entire application.

The long-term value of healthcare voice AI will not come from making agents sound indistinguishable from humans.

It will come from making them reliable enough to handle clearly defined administrative workflows while knowing exactly when to involve a human.

For developers, that means investing as much effort in integrations, security, observability, and failure handling as in the AI conversation itself.

Because in healthcare, a convincing response isn't enough.

The system has to get the underlying action right.

What do you think is the hardest part of building production-ready healthcare voice agents: real-time latency, EHR interoperability, data privacy, or reliable human escalation?

Building Connected Pharmaceutical Manufacturing: The Role of AIoT in Operational Data

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pharmaceutical manufacturing depends on coordination between several activities: material handling, equipment operation, production, quality checks, and batch documentation.
  • According to recent reports, when departments rely on separate systems or manual records, understanding the complete manufacturing workflow can become difficult.
  • Imagine a production team trying to check whether a material is available, whether the required equipment is ready, and whether the relevant production records have been updated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pharmaceutical manufacturing depends on coordination between several activities: material handling, equipment operation, production, quality checks, and batch documentation. Each activity generates information, but that information is not always connected.

According to recent reports, when departments rely on separate systems or manual records, understanding the complete manufacturing workflow can become difficult. This is one of the challenges that Industrial IoT and AIoT are trying to address.

The Challenge: Data Exists, but Is It Connected?

Imagine a production team trying to check whether a material is available, whether the required equipment is ready, and whether the relevant production records have been updated.

The information may exist, but it could be spread across inventory software, equipment records, spreadsheets, and quality systems.

This creates several practical challenges:.

Delays in finding operational information.

Limited visibility into material and equipment movement.

Difficulty connecting production events with relevant records.

More effort when reviewing historical activities.

The problem is not simply collecting more data. It is making existing information easier to connect and interpret.

Industry observers note that the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) connects equipment, sensors, and other physical assets so they can generate and share operational data. AIoT builds on this concept by using artificial intelligence to help analyse connected information and identify patterns.

In pharmaceutical manufacturing, different technologies can contribute to this approach:.

These technologies can support the identification and tracking of materials, equipment, and other assets. Their suitability depends on the facility layout, tracking requirements, and operating environment.

Sources indicate that sensors can collect information about environmental conditions or equipment status. For example, temperature and humidity measurements may be relevant in areas where environmental conditions need to be monitored.

Edge computing allows some data processing to take place closer to the devices generating the information. This can be useful where timely processing or reduced dependence on continuous cloud connectivity is crucial.

Sources indicate that analytical tools can help identify patterns, unusual changes, or operational trends. Their outputs should support qualified personnel rather than replace established quality and operational decision-making processes.

Integration With Existing Manufacturing Systems.

One important consideration is how upcoming technologies will work with systems already used by pharmaceutical manufacturers.

MES: Manufacturing Execution Systems.

ERP: Enterprise Resource Planning.

LIMS: Laboratory Information Management Systems.

QMS: Quality Management Systems.

If connected devices operate independently from these systems, organisations may end up creating another information silo. A better starting point is to map the existing workflow, identify information gaps, and determine which systems need to exchange data.

Data integrity, access permissions, validation requirements, and clear responsibility for reviewing information should also be considered during implementation.

Start With a Practical Use Case.

A pharmaceutical facility does not need to connect every asset and process at once. A small pilot can provide a more manageable starting point.

Sources indicate that for example, a manufacturer could select one equipment-tracking or environmental-monitoring workflow. The team could then assess:.

What information needs to be collected?

Which devices or sensors are appropriate?

Where should the information be stored?

Which existing systems need access to it?

How will data accuracy be checked?

Who is responsible for responding to alerts?

This approach helps establish whether the technology addresses a real operational problem before expanding it across the facility.

AIoT in pharmaceutical manufacturing is not simply about adding connected devices. Its value lies in connecting information from different parts of the operation and making that information more useful.

This is the broader direction explored by PharmaFlux AI, which focuses on AIoT and industrial intelligence for pharmaceutical operations.

Recent findings suggest that for manufacturers exploring digital transformation, the most key question may not be how many sensors they can install. It may be how effectively they can connect the information they already depend on.

Better visibility begins with better-connected processes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.
  • Industry observers note that if you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline.
  • The inference engine speaks the policy of step N.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR, because you have models to train and we respect that:.

Async RL just got a lot cheaper. Read on.

Industry observers note that if you read our previous post on the landscape of async RL training, you already know the punchline. Every async RL library, regardless of how it spells "actor model" or which color its NCCL backend is painted, eventually trips over the same root: weight synchronization.

The inference engine speaks the policy of step N. The trainer just finished step N+1. The fresh weights have to get from one side to the other before the inference engine starts drifting hopelessly off-policy. This sits on the critical path whether you are running sync or async: a blocking transfer is wasted idle compute of GPUs not generating tokens. With a sparse delta path you collapse that idle time into seconds, and the trainer does not even have to wait for the inference engine to be ready: it just publishes "weights ready" and uploads the weights to the shared bucket the moment its optimizer step finishes, while the inference engine fetches on its own time.

Fireworks put a very memorable number on this in their post Frontier RL Is Cheaper Than You Think: for a frontier 1T-parameter checkpoint at fp8 (their setting), a full snapshot is 1024 GiB, and that is what conventional wisdom says you have to ship every time you revision your rollout fleet. That is the kind of number that gets people to start drawing diagrams with mega-clusters, RDMA fabrics, and dedicated cross-region links. Their measured average delta between adjacent checkpoints lands at 20.3 GiB, or 1.98% of the full model, and "more than 98% of weights in bf16 format remain bit-equivalent between consecutive checkpoints".

Cursor's Composer 2 report tells a parallel story. They run training and inference in different regions and stitch them together with a shared S3 bucket (their exact words), into which the trainer uploads compressed weight diffs every training step. Each cluster independently downloads and reconstructs from the shared delta chain, "requiring no direct connectivity to the training cluster". The two sides never speak to each other about parameters directly. The bucket is the wire.

Both papers agree on three things, and we want to repeat them slowly, because the rest of this post is essentially a faithful open source translation:.

Industry observers note that the only thing missing was a version of this story that you can pip install. So we wrote one.

Sources indicate that before we wire anything up, it is worth understanding why this whole game is even winnable. The "98% of weights do not change" claim sounds suspiciously like one of those numbers that works in the demo and falls apart in the wild. It is not. It falls out of how bf16 arithmetic works at the learning rates RL uses.

Recent findings suggest that A bf16 number has 7 mantissa bits. Between two consecutive powers of two, there are exactly 27=1282^7 = 12827=128 representable values, so the spacing between adjacent bf16 numbers around ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ is roughly ∣w∣⋅2−7|w| \cdot 2^{-7}∣w∣⋅2−7. An enhancement gets absorbed by the bf16 cast whenever it sits below half of that spacing, i.e., when ∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256|\Delta w| < |w|/256∣Δw∣<∣w∣/256. This is the "bf16 visibility threshold" PULSE plots in their Figure 3.

According to recent reports, now look at what Adam does. At an RL learning rate of, say, 3×10−63 \times 10^{-6}3×10−6, the upgrade to a single weight is: Δw=−η⋅m^v^+ϵ\Delta w = -\eta \cdot \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon}Δw=−η⋅v^​+ϵm^​.

In a recent development, the normalized step m^/(v^+ϵ)\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)m^/(v^​+ϵ) is roughly order one, so ∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6|\Delta w| \approx \eta \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}∣Δw∣≈η≈3×10−6. For most weights, ∣w∣|w|∣w∣ sits somewhere around 10−210^{-2}10−2 to 10−110^{-1}10−1 (PULSE reports a median of 0.019 for representative LLM weights). The threshold ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256 at that magnitude is around 4×10−54 \times 10^{-5}4×10−5 to 4×10−44 \times 10^{-4}4×10−4, which is bigger than the update.

According to recent reports, in other words: the optimizer is whispering, and bf16 cannot hear it. The update gets absorbed by rounding, the byte representation of www does not change, and from the inference engine's perspective, this weight did not move. Multiply that by a few hundred million parameters, and you get the >99% sparsity number, for free, with zero approximation.

According to recent reports, this is exactly the argument made formal in the PULSE paper (Mihai & Belilovsky, 2026). They define two thresholds. The absorption bound 10η10\eta10η is the conservative worst case for an Adam patch, and the effective bound η\etaη is the regime you actually live in. The bf16 visibility threshold is ∣w∣/256|w|/256∣w∣/256. Whenever the update sits below the visibility threshold, it gets absorbed, and the bf16 byte does not change. Their Figure 3 plots both bounds against a cloud of representative LLM weights, and the conclusion is unambiguous: at η=3×10−6\eta = 3 \times 10^{-6}η=3×10−6, the absorption bound itself already sits below the visibility threshold for almost every weight in the model. They measure this empirically across Qwen2.5 (0.5B/1.5B/7B), Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B, and consistently find a mean per-step sparsity of ~99%, with a standard deviation of 0.2 to 0.4% over 400 training steps. The worst-case step stays above 98%. So <1% changed is not a lucky measurement; it is what the arithmetic guarantees.

We do not have to predict this analytically (and indeed, we tried predicting the change mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, but recall was a sad 30%, more on that later). We just need to observe which bytes flipped. That is a tiny boolean tensor per parameter, computed right around the optimizer step.

Here is where the second piece of the story comes in, and where this post stops being a translation of Fireworks/Cursor and starts being a Hugging Face thing.

Industry observers note that A Bucket is a repo type on the Hub designed for high-frequency object storage. No commit ceremony, no PR workflow, no LFS quirks. You add files, you list files, you download files. The Python interface is two functions:.

Recent findings suggest that that is it. Two function calls and your weights are in flight.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, buckets are backed by Xet, the Hub's content-defined chunking storage layer. Xet looks at every file you upload, slices it into chunks based on its actual content (not fixed offsets), and deduplicates against everything already in the bucket. The practical upshot, which is delightful in this context, is that even if we were too lazy to write the sparse encoding and just uploaded full anchors every step, Xet would still only transfer the changed chunks. Sparse encoding + Xet stack: we pay for what moved, and we pay for it once.

This is the open source equivalent of the "shared S3 bucket" both Fireworks and Cursor reach for, except the storage layer already knows about content hashing, your existing HF token already has permission, and it composes natively with the rest of the stack (Spaces, datasets, models).

The full architecture has exactly three boxes and one shared substrate:.

The property to internalize, the one Cursor's paper sells hard and that holds verbatim here: the trainer and the rollout server never talk to each other about weights. They exchange a tiny POST containing {"repo_id": ..., "filename": ...}, and that is the entire control plane. The actual byte transfer happens between each side and the bucket, in parallel, with no shared network fabric.

The trainer writes. Replicas read. The Hub does the plumbing.

According to recent reports, now we can open the hood. The protocol has four parts: a wire format, a bucket layout, a 30 line vLLM extension, and a trainer side change detector. It is honestly less code than it sounds.

According to recent reports, we picked safetensors for the on-disk and on-wire format. It is already the canonical checkpoint format on the Hub, every reasonable framework can read it, and the header carries arbitrary string metadata. That metadata field is where we hide the protocol.

There are two kinds of files in the bucket.

Anchors look like a normal checkpoint: one tensor per parameter, full bf16 weights, written every NNN syncs (we default to N=10N=10N=10).

Recent findings suggest that deltas are the interesting bit. For each parameter that actually changed, we store two entries: a flat int32 tensor of element indices, and a bf16 tensor of values at those indices.

A few nice consequences of this choice:.

It has been revealed that the cadence is straightforward: anchor every Nth step, delta in between. Both end up in the same bucket under anchors/ and deltas/ prefixes. Each upcoming inference replica only needs to grab the most recent anchor and then replay the deltas since.

Industry observers note that the trainer needs to know which bf16 elements actually flipped. We do this with a tiny BF16ChangeDetector that registers a pre-step and post-step hook on the optimizer:.

The actual code in the PR has a bit more plumbing (matching optimizer param objects to model params via data_ptr(), because Accelerate wraps them as different Python objects), but the idea fits on a napkin: snapshot, step, diff.

This is ground truth. We tried the more elegant path of predicting the mask from Adam's mmm and vvv statistics, using the bf16 ULP threshold directly. It works in principle. In practice, recall was around 30%, which means we would have shipped a delta missing two thirds of the actual updates. Adam's normalization is messy enough that the analytical threshold is not tight. So we just compare bytes. It costs one bf16 CPU snapshot of the model on the trainer side, which we are willing to pay.

The four phases of the newly introduced _sync_weight flow are:.

The line that matters is the parenthesis. Inference was paused for 1.1 seconds. The remaining 9.4 seconds were spent uploading, which occurred while the rollout server was still generating tokens. With NCCL, we were paying the full sync time as pause time. Here we are paying for it as background time.

vLLM has a clean abstraction for this called WeightTransferEngine. We implement a DeltaWeightTransferEngine whose receive_weights method is, in spirit:.

According to recent reports, we register it via vLLM's --worker-extension-cls flag, which means no fork of vLLM is required. You install TRL into the same image as vLLM, point the CLI at our class, and you are done.

Worth mentioning: vLLM itself has an in-flight effort to land sparse weight transfer natively, vllm-project/vllm#40096. It adds receive_sparse_weights() and trainer_send_sparse_weights() directly on the WeightTransferEngine base class, with patches encoded as (indices, values) and applied in place via index_copy_(), removing the GPU/CPU validation roundtrip entirely. The PR reports a transfer of 0.16 MB in 0.40 ms for a sparse patch on Qwen3-1.7B versus 942 MB in 192 ms for a full dense send.

According to recent reports, one honest caveat in our implementation on the inference side: we keep a CPU bf16 snapshot of the model so we can reconstruct full tensors from sparse (indices, values) patches, because load_weights in vLLM today expects full tensors. Once #40096 (or its successor) lands and exposes an in-place sparse load_weights path, we can apply the indices directly on the GPU and drop the snapshot!

According to recent reports, this is the part we are smug about. Everything we have described so far works on your laptop, but the point of routing weights through a Hub bucket is that the trainer and the rollout server do not have to live anywhere near each other. So we ran a fully disaggregated training with three machines, none of which share a network:.

Setting this up is genuinely a few hf CLI calls. The vLLM Space's Dockerfile is essentially the upstream vLLM image plus pip install trl@... plus the entrypoint:.

And kick off training from anywhere on the planet that can talk HTTPS:.

It has been revealed that the trainer never opens a port. The Space never sees the trainer's IP. The Wordle environment does not know either of them exists. They all talk to the Hub. Training converged on the immediate-EOS sanity check, then on real Wordle rollouts: reward went up, delta payloads stayed in the 20 to 35 MB band, and the inference-paused window per sync stayed around a second. The full run logs are linked in the companion PR.

A few things, and we think they are substantial.

In a recent development, async RL training without a cluster. If you have one GPU and a Hugging Face account, you can now do real disaggregated training. Your trainer is on the GPU; your rollout fleet lives in Spaces; your environment lives in another Space; weights move through a bucket. This used to require either a colocated setup (with all the throughput compromises that brings) or a real cluster with shared networking. It does not anymore.

Industry observers note that multi-replica inference, for free. Stand up two vLLM Spaces, or ten. They all pull from the same bucket. Xet content-addresses storage so consecutive anchors share chunks at rest (which keeps your bucket from blowing up), and the Hub's edge cache makes repeated downloads of the same file cheap to serve. Want a globally distributed rollout fleet? That is now a small DevOps exercise, not a research project.

A wire format you can debug with your existing tools. A delta is a safetensors file. You can safe_open it from a notebook, list its keys, inspect the indices, compute the sparsity yourself. We have spent enough hours in tcpdump on opaque NCCL streams to appreciate this.

A path to frontier scale. The 20 to 35 MB number is for Qwen3-0.6B. The interesting question is what the curve looks like once you turn the dial up. Let us do the napkin math.

It has been revealed that take Llama-3.1-405B. In bf16 that is 810 GB on disk. PULSE measures ~99% mean per-step sparsity at RL learning rates, so the actual delta sits around 1% of the parameters. Their deployment-measured encoding hits 108 MB on a 7B model, which is the ~130× reduction PULSE reports. Scaled linearly to 405B, the delta lands at roughly 6 GB per step.

What does that buy you in wall-clock? NCCL is fast inside a cluster, sure. Assume a generous 100 GB/s aggregate broadcast bandwidth (multi-node, RDMA, the works). A full sync is 810 GB / 100 GB/s ≈ 8 seconds of inference pause, every step. With the delta path, the trainer streams 6 GB to a bucket in the background while generation keeps running, and the rollout server's actual paused window is just the apply step, which on this scale lands at a couple of seconds. So even before we leave the cluster, delta cuts the visible pause by 4× and the bytes on the wire by ~130×.

Sources indicate that now leave the cluster. NCCL straight up does not work across clouds. Once you want a rollout fleet in us-east, another in eu-west, maybe one in a Hugging Face Space, the bucket-based path is the only path. At 1 GB/s of usable internet bandwidth, a single full broadcast would take 13 minutes; the delta does it in 6 seconds.

For a 1 TB-class model in the Fireworks framing, their own measured numbers show 20.3 GiB deltas vs the 1024 GiB full snapshot, a ~50× reduction. PULSE's tighter, sparse encoding would push that further (extrapolating ~15 GB per delta, closer to ~65×). Either way, you are in a regime where shipping weights through commodity object storage stops being a hack and starts being the only sensible architecture.

#103561. The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1122 w)
